title: Motivation: Maslow & Herzberg
blurb: Climb Maslow's five levels in the right order, sort Herzberg's hygiene factors from his motivators, and use both to diagnose and fix low motivation.
question: After complaints about pay on a hospital IT upgrade, the analysts are given a pay rise. The complaints stop, but energy and ideas don't improve. Meanwhile a contractor who fears his contract won't be renewed ignores every offer of interesting new work. Using Maslow and Herzberg, explain both reactions and what the project manager should do.

teach.h: Two lenses on what motivates people
teach.body: Motivation is the drive that makes people start, direct and sustain effort. Two classic models help a project manager work out why someone isn't motivated and what will help. Maslow says needs form a hierarchy: lower needs must be met before higher ones motivate. Herzberg says two separate sets of factors are at work: hygiene factors that prevent dissatisfaction, and motivators that create satisfaction. Used together, they stop a PM wasting effort on the wrong fix.

levels.label: Love/belonging (social)
levels.sub: Acceptance, being part of the team

levels.label: Safety
levels.sub: Job security, stability, a safe workplace

levels.label: Physiological
levels.sub: Food, rest, warmth: pay that covers them

teach.caption: Read it from the bottom up: physiological, safety, love/belonging, esteem, self-actualisation.

teach.body: Lower needs must be largely met before higher ones motivate. A need that is satisfied no longer motivates, so the next level up takes over. People can also drop back down: rumours of redundancy push someone's focus straight back to safety, whatever stretch work is on offer. For a project manager the lesson is diagnosis first: find the level each person is at, fix any unmet lower need, then motivate through the next level up.

teach.body: Herzberg found that the things that make people unhappy at work are different from the things that make them motivated. HYGIENE factors (pay, conditions, policies, supervision, job security, relationships) prevent dissatisfaction when right, but don't motivate. Get them wrong and people are dissatisfied. MOTIVATORS (achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement, growth) create satisfaction and real motivation. So the opposite of dissatisfaction is not satisfaction: it is simply no dissatisfaction.

teach.caption: Iterative projects build in motivators (achievement and recognition at every demo). In long linear phases the PM has to create them, for example by marking milestones.

teach.h: How the two models line up
head: Maslow level
Herzberg
Project example
teach.caption: Broadly: Maslow's lower needs behave like Herzberg's hygiene factors, and the higher needs like his motivators.

teach.body: The analysts complained about pay, so a pay rise was agreed. Complaints stopped, but energy didn't rise: pay is a hygiene factor. The PM then gives Sam ownership of the data migration (responsibility), credits her by name in the board report (recognition) and shows progress at each milestone (achievement). Engagement climbs. Ravi, a contractor, ignores new work because he fears non-renewal: an unmet safety need. Once the PM confirms his extension, he engages.

teach.text: Classic confusions: pay is a HYGIENE factor in Herzberg, not a motivator, so fixing pay, conditions or policies removes dissatisfaction but won't by itself motivate. Recognition, responsibility and the work itself are MOTIVATORS. And Maslow's order is fixed: physiological, safety, love/belonging, esteem, self-actualisation. Exam options swap safety and belonging, or put esteem at the base.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name the model and its structure: Maslow's five levels in order, or Herzberg's two sets of factors.
Explain the key principle: lower needs first (Maslow); hygiene prevents dissatisfaction while motivators motivate (Herzberg).
Diagnose the scenario: which need or factor is missing for this person?
Recommend a specific PM action: fix the unmet lower need or hygiene factor, then use motivators such as responsibility and recognition.
Link to the project: higher commitment, better performance, retention of key people.
Maslow, bottom to top: physiological, safety, love/belonging, esteem, self-actualisation.
Lower needs must be largely met before higher ones motivate; a met need no longer motivates.
Herzberg hygiene: pay, conditions, policies, supervision, job security, relationships.
Herzberg motivators: achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement, growth.
Fix hygiene to stop dissatisfaction; use motivators to create motivation.

summary: You can now state Maslow's five needs in order and Herzberg's hygiene factors and motivators. You can also use both models to diagnose why a team member isn't motivated and choose the action most likely to help.

A.q: In Maslow's hierarchy of needs, which level sits directly above safety?
A.why: From the bottom: physiological, safety, love/belonging (social), esteem, self-actualisation. Love/belonging comes straight after safety.

whyNot.0: Esteem sits above love/belonging, not directly above safety.
whyNot.1: Physiological needs are the base, below safety.

A.q: According to Herzberg, which of these is a HYGIENE factor?
A.why: Job security is a hygiene factor: when it is missing people are dissatisfied, but having it doesn't in itself motivate.

whyNot.1: Recognition is one of Herzberg's motivators.

A.q: Complete the statement: in Herzberg's theory, when hygiene factors are right they ____.
A.why: Good hygiene factors remove dissatisfaction; they don't create motivation. Motivators do that.

whyNot.0: Lasting motivation comes from motivators such as achievement and responsibility.
whyNot.1: Hygiene and motivators are separate; both are needed.
whyNot.2: Recognition is a motivator and remains important however good the hygiene factors are.

B.q: A project analyst has just been told her contract may not be renewed when the project ends. According to Maslow, why is offering her a stretch assignment unlikely to motivate her right now?
options: Stretch work only motivates people at the physiological level
Her unmet safety need takes priority over the higher needs
Maslow says recognition matters more than security at work
Self-actualisation must be met before safety can motivate
B.why: Job security is a safety need. Until it is largely met, higher-level motivators such as growth and challenge have little pull.

whyNot.0: Stretch work appeals to self-actualisation, the top level, not physiological needs.
whyNot.2: Maslow puts safety BELOW esteem: it must be met first.
whyNot.3: This reverses the hierarchy: lower needs come first.

B.q: Which list contains ONLY Herzberg motivators?
B.why: Recognition, growth and achievement are all motivators.

whyNot.2: Company policies are a hygiene factor.

B.q: After a pay review, complaints from a bid team stop, but their energy and ideas don't increase. Which explanation is BEST?
options: Herzberg: pay is a hygiene factor
McGregor: the team is Theory X
Herzberg: pay is a key motivator
B.why: Fixing a hygiene factor removes dissatisfaction (so complaints stop) but doesn't create motivation (so energy stays flat).

whyNot.1: Pay mainly supports the lower needs (physiological and safety), not self-actualisation.
whyNot.2: McGregor describes managers' assumptions, not a team type, and doesn't explain this pattern.
whyNot.3: If pay were a motivator, energy would have risen. Herzberg classes it as hygiene.

C.q: On a two-year rail signalling project, an experienced engineer is reliable but clearly bored. Pay and conditions are good. Which action BEST applies Herzberg's motivators?
options: Arrange a further pay rise above the market rate
Tighten supervision to keep the engineer focused
Give ownership of a challenging work package
Improve the site welfare facilities and canteen
C.why: Ownership of challenging work brings responsibility, achievement and the work itself: three motivators.

whyNot.0: Pay is a hygiene factor and is already good; more of it won't cure boredom.
whyNot.1: Supervision is a hygiene factor, and tighter control is more likely to demotivate.
whyNot.3: Welfare facilities are working conditions: a hygiene factor.

C.q:
Which TWO statements about Maslow's hierarchy are correct?
1. Lower needs must largely be met before higher needs motivate
2. Esteem sits at the base of the hierarchy
3. A need that is satisfied no longer motivates
4. Safety is the highest level
C.why: Statements 1 and 3 are core Maslow principles.

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: physiological needs are the base; esteem is fourth.
whyNot.2: Both are wrong: esteem is not the base and safety is not the top.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: self-actualisation is the highest level.

C.q: A remote member of a hybrid project team says she feels cut off from colleagues and is never invited to the informal catch-ups. Using Maslow, which need is MOST clearly unmet, and what should the PM do?
options: Safety: guarantee her next role in writing
Self-actualisation: send her on a course
Belonging: include her in team rituals
C.why: Feeling cut off and excluded is an unmet love/belonging (social) need. Deliberate inclusion in team rituals and catch-ups addresses it.

whyNot.0: Nothing suggests overwork; her issue is social exclusion.
whyNot.1: She hasn't raised job security; the problem is belonging.
whyNot.2: Development serves self-actualisation, but a lower unmet need (belonging) comes first.

reteach.title: Think of a holiday hotel
reteach.question: Picture your last hotel stay. What would make you complain, and what would make you rave about it to friends? Are they the same things?

blocks.body: A dirty room, a cold shower or a rude receptionist makes you complain. But a clean room and hot water never make you tell friends it was amazing: you simply expect them. Those are Herzberg's hygiene factors. What you rave about is the sunset view, the cookery class, the staff who remembered your name: the motivators. Maslow adds the order: nobody enjoys the spa if they have nowhere safe to sleep.

blocks.text: On a project, pay and conditions are the clean room: fix them to stop complaints, but motivate with achievement, recognition, responsibility and growth.

explain.body: From the bottom: physiological (food, rest), safety (security, stability), love/belonging (acceptance, being part of a group), esteem (recognition, respect) and self-actualisation (reaching your potential).

explain.caption: Memory hook: 'Please Send Lunch Every Saturday', climbing from the base.

test.q: Which shows Maslow's levels in the correct order, starting from the bottom?
test.why: The order from the base is physiological, safety, love/belonging, esteem, self-actualisation.

whyNot.1: Safety comes before belonging, not after it.
whyNot.2: Physiological needs are the base, below safety.
whyNot.3: Belonging comes before esteem, not after it.

explain.body: Diagnose first. If a lower need is unmet (overwork, job insecurity, exclusion), fix it, because higher motivators won't land until you do. Once lower needs are met, motivate through the next level up: recognition for esteem, stretch work for self-actualisation.

test.q: A team member's basic needs and job security are met, and they feel fully part of the team. According to Maslow, what is MOST likely to motivate them next?
options: More team social events and outings
test.why: With physiological, safety and belonging needs met, the next level is esteem: recognition and respect.

whyNot.0: Job security (safety) is already met, so it no longer motivates.
whyNot.1: Belonging is already met; more social events add little motivation.
whyNot.3: Working hours relate to the physiological level, which is already met.

explain.body: Hygiene factors and motivators sit on separate scales. Good hygiene takes people from dissatisfied to neutral. Motivators take people from neutral to motivated. That is why fixing pay stops complaints but doesn't create energy.

test.q: In Herzberg's model, what is the opposite of 'dissatisfaction'?
test.why: Herzberg's key insight: removing the causes of dissatisfaction leads to NO dissatisfaction, not to satisfaction. Satisfaction comes from motivators.

whyNot.0: Satisfaction sits on the separate motivator scale; it is not the opposite of dissatisfaction.
whyNot.2: Motivation comes from motivators, not from fixing hygiene factors.
whyNot.3: Self-actualisation is Maslow's top level, not part of Herzberg's model.

explain.body: First check the hygiene factors (pay, conditions, policies, supervision, job security, relationships) and fix anything causing dissatisfaction. Then build in motivators: give responsibility, recognise achievement, make the work itself interesting and offer growth and advancement.

test.q: A PM's team complains about cramped desks and slow laptops. What will fixing these MOST likely achieve?
options: Removal of a source of dissatisfaction
A lasting rise in team motivation
Less need for any recognition from now on
test.why: Desks and laptops are working conditions, a hygiene factor. Fixing them removes dissatisfaction but won't motivate on its own.

whyNot.1: Lasting motivation comes from motivators, not hygiene factors.
whyNot.2: Equipment and conditions relate to lower-level needs, not esteem or self-actualisation.
whyNot.3: Recognition is a motivator and stays important.
